prompt: Which Redis structure and commands fit best?
scenario: A game needs a global leaderboard of 5 million players: update a player's score many times a minute, show the top 10, and show any player's rank.

options.text: A sorted set: ZINCRBY for updates, ZRANGE ... REV for the top 10, ZREVRANK for rank
A list: LPUSH each new score, then LRANGE the whole list and sort the scores in the app
A hash: HSET player score for updates, then HGETALL and sort it in the app
A HyperLogLog of players: PFADD on each update and PFCOUNT for the ranking

explanation: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score with O(log N) updates and rank lookups, exactly a leaderboard. A list has no ordering by score, so you'd sort 5 million entries per request. A hash stores scores but HGETALL plus an app-side sort is O(N) per read and blocks the server on a huge key. A HyperLogLog only estimates how many distinct players exist; it can't store scores or ranks.

prompt: You need the approximate number of unique daily visitors (about 10 million) using as little memory as possible. Which structure?

options.text: HyperLogLog (PFADD / PFCOUNT)
Set of visitor IDs (SADD / SCARD)
String counter per visit (INCR)
Stream of visit events (XADD / XLEN)

explanation: HyperLogLog estimates distinct counts in at most 12 KB with about 0.81% error. A set is exact but stores every member, costing hundreds of megabytes. INCR counts visits, not unique visitors, because repeat visits increment it again. A stream stores every event, using even more memory than a set.

prompt: Which statements about Redis streams versus lists as queues are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stream consumer groups track which entries each consumer has acknowledged with XACK
Entries in a stream remain after being read, so they can be replayed
A popped list item stays in the list until acknowledged
Streams give each entry a time-based ID

explanation: Streams are append-only logs: reading doesn't remove entries, consumer groups track pending and acknowledged entries, and IDs are time-based (milliseconds-sequence). A popped list item is removed immediately; if the worker crashes, it's lost unless you use a pattern like LMOVE into a processing list.

prompt: Why are the sessions no longer expiring?
scenario: Sessions are created with SET session:abc <json> EX 1800. A new feature updates the session on every request with SET session:abc <newjson>. Memory starts growing steadily and old sessions never disappear.

options.text: A plain SET without EX or KEEPTTL clears the TTL, so updated sessions live forever
Redis only expires keys once memory is full, so idle sessions just keep accumulating
TTLs only work on hash keys, so the JSON string sessions can never expire
The EX value must be given in milliseconds, so EX 1800 is silently ignored

explanation: Overwriting a key with a plain SET clears its TTL. Use SET ... EX 1800 again or SET ... KEEPTTL. Expiry happens on access and via a background sampling cycle, regardless of memory; evicting when full is a separate mechanism. TTLs apply to keys of any type, strings included. EX takes seconds and is never ignored; PX takes milliseconds.

prompt: What does TTL return for a key that exists but has no expiry?

options.text: nil

explanation: -1 means the key exists with no TTL. -2 means the key doesn't exist. 0 would mean it is about to expire, not that it has no expiry. TTL returns an integer, never nil.

prompt: Roughly how many writes could a crash lose with each configuration?
scenario: A Redis instance takes 2,000 writes a second. Config A: RDB snapshot every 10 minutes, no AOF. Config B: AOF with appendfsync everysec.

options.text: A: up to about 1.2 million; B: about 2,000
A: about 2,000; B: up to about 1.2 million
Both lose nothing
A: up to about 20,000; B: zero

explanation: RDB loses everything since the last snapshot: up to 600 s × 2,000 = 1.2 million writes. AOF everysec fsyncs once a second, so about one second, roughly 2,000 writes. Swapping them reverses the mechanisms. Neither is lossless. 20,000 corresponds to 10 seconds, not 10 minutes, and everysec is not zero loss; only appendfsync always comes close.

prompt: How does BGSAVE write a snapshot without stopping Redis from serving requests?

options.text: It forks a child that writes the file while sharing pages with the parent via copy-on-write
It takes a brief lock on each key while copying it, so only one key pauses at a time
It asks a replica to write the snapshot file, so the primary never does the work
It replays the AOF into a fresh file on a background thread, without touching memory

explanation: fork() plus copy-on-write lets the child see a frozen view while the parent keeps serving; only pages modified during the save are duplicated. Redis doesn't lock keys, one at a time or otherwise, for snapshots. BGSAVE runs on the instance it's called on, not a replica. Replaying the AOF is not how RDB works; an AOF rewrite is a different operation, and it also forks.

prompt: Why does this fail, and what is the fix?
scenario: In Redis Cluster, a script runs MGET cart:42 profile:42 and gets a CROSSSLOT error.

options.text: The keys hash to different slots; use a hash tag like {user:42}:cart and {user:42}:profile
MGET isn't supported in Redis Cluster at all; send separate GETs from the script
The cluster has fewer than 16,384 nodes, so some slots have no owner for these keys
The keys have different TTLs, and multi-key commands require matching expiry times

explanation: Multi-key commands require all keys in one slot. With a hash tag, only the part in braces is hashed, so both keys land together. MGET works in Cluster when keys share a slot. 16,384 is the number of slots, not nodes, and every slot is assigned to some node. TTLs have nothing to do with slot placement.

prompt: A Redis primary acknowledges a write and crashes before sending it to its replica. Sentinel promotes the replica. What happens to the write?

options.text: It is lost, because replication is asynchronous by default
The replica fetches it from the dead primary's memory on promotion
Sentinel replays it from its own log of acknowledged writes
The client library is told by Sentinel to retry it automatically

explanation: Async replication means acknowledged writes can be lost on failover; WAIT narrows the window but doesn't eliminate it. A crashed process's memory is gone. Sentinel monitors and coordinates failover; it doesn't store data. The client already got a success reply, so nothing tells it to retry.

prompt: What is the most likely cause?
scenario: Every few minutes, all Redis calls from every service spike from under 1 ms to 2 seconds at the same moment. SLOWLOG shows KEYS user:* taking about 1,900 ms. The instance holds 40 million keys.

options.text: KEYS walks all 40 million keys on the one command thread, blocking every client; use SCAN
The network is dropping packets every few minutes, so calls wait on TCP retransmits
Too many I/O threads are configured, so they contend with the main thread for CPU
Persistence is disabled, so Redis rebuilds its data from scratch every few minutes

explanation: Commands execute one at a time, so an O(N) command over 40 million keys stalls everything for its duration. SCAN iterates in small batches between other clients' commands. Packet loss wouldn't line up exactly with a slow-log entry. I/O threads handle socket reads and writes, not command execution, and wouldn't make KEYS slow. Disabling persistence means nothing is reloaded except on restart, and it doesn't make commands slow.

prompt: One command in a MULTI/EXEC block fails at runtime (INCR on a non-numeric value). What happens to the other commands?

options.text: They still execute; Redis transactions don't roll back
All of them are rolled back, as in a database transaction
The server automatically restarts the whole transaction
Only the commands queued before the failing one run

explanation: MULTI/EXEC guarantees the queued commands run without interleaving, but a runtime error in one doesn't undo or skip the others. There is no rollback. Redis never automatically retries a transaction. Commands after the failure still run too.

prompt: Releasing a lock with GET (check the token) then DEL from the client is unsafe. Which approaches are safe? Select all that apply.

options.text: A Lua script that compares the token and deletes in one atomic step
WATCH the lock key, check the token, then MULTI / DEL / EXEC and retry if aborted
DEL the key directly without checking the token, since the lock has a TTL anyway
GET then DEL as before, but pipelined so both commands go in one round trip

explanation: A Lua script runs atomically, so nobody can take the lock between the check and the delete. WATCH aborts the transaction if the key changes after your check, giving the same safety optimistically. Deleting without checking can remove a lock someone else now holds, TTL or not. Pipelining sends the two commands together but they are still separate, and the client must decide on the GET result before sending DEL, so the race narrows but never closes.
